title: In the bleak midwinter (Rossetti, 1872)
hookLine: what can I give him, poor as I am? give my heart
tomorrow: can a worn-out world still be charged with something?

lines: YOUR SHARE IS MORE THAN YOU HAVE.
NOTHING TO BUY THAT FIXES IT.
cards: A friend's birthday, and the group chat is splitting the cost of a gift, and your share is more than your account holds. Or someone you love is going through something no store sells a fix for.
Empty hands are an old problem.

Christina Rossetti, an English poet, wrote a Christmas poem that walks straight into it, starting in the coldest weather she could find: earth hard as iron, water like a stone, “Snow had fallen, snow on snow.”

teach.h: A SMALL PLACE FOR A GREAT GUEST.
teach.b: Into that cold she sets a newborn. Heaven can't hold him, the poem says, nor earth sustain him, and yet a stable was enough. A small place for a great guest.

Then the last verse asks the question: “What can I give Him, Poor as I am?” Rossetti looks around the stable for answers. “If I were a shepherd I would bring a lamb; If I were a Wise Man I would do my part.”
She's thinking of the people in the Gospel stories who came with something. Luke's shepherds “came with haste.” Matthew's wise men opened their treasures: “gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.”
But she is neither. No lamb, no gold.
And then the turn, as plain as a child's answer: “Yet what I can I give Him: Give my heart.” Notice what she doesn't say.
She doesn't call the lamb and the gold useless, or say the shepherds had it wrong. Those are real gifts. She just finds that the poorest person in the poem still has one thing to bring.

teach.h: A HEART, GIVEN AS IT IS.
teach.b: A heart, given as it is, on a cold night, to someone who came into a small place.
Nobody arrives at that stable with enough. They arrive with what they have.

how: Choirs and congregations sing In the Bleak Midwinter at Christmas, set to music that came after Rossetti wrote the poem.

games.q: what does “in the bleak midwinter” mean?
o: a carol about the wise men's long journey through snow
Rossetti's cold Christmas poem ending on the gift of a heart
a hymn about the longest night of the winter solstice

games.q: who brings what — tap the pairs.

s: In the bleak midwinter is a line from the Christmas Gospels
it's Christina Rossetti's poem. the Gospels give her the shepherds and the wise men.
Rossetti says gifts like the lamb and the gold don't matter
they're real gifts. she just finds the one gift the poorest still has.
the poem opens in deep cold, snow on snow
earth hard as iron, water like a stone, and a newborn set in the middle of it.

games.q: a classmate's family is going through a hard month, and everyone is chipping in money. you can't. what fits Rossetti's last verse?
o: stay out of it; with no money, there's nothing you can really bring.
give what you do have: show up, help out, write them a note.
borrow money so your gift matches what everyone else gave.
games.why: Rossetti doesn't say the lamb and the gold don't matter. she finds the one thing the poorest still has, and brings it: give my heart.

practice: If there's paper near you, write Rossetti's question at the top: what can I give? Under it, write one thing you could give today that costs nothing, an hour, a call, your full attention, and the name of who it's for.
Then rest your hands open on the page for the rest of the sit.
